text: Ψάλλει τι τῷ πνεύματι. Scite Theodoret.: Πνεῦμα, τὸ χάρισμα καλεῖ· νοῦν δὲ, τὴν σαφήνειαν τῶν λεγομένων. Spiritum, vocat donum: mentem autem, rerum quæ dicuntur explanationem. Nec aliter Chrys. hom. 35: Αἴτει μὴ γλώττης ἔχειν χάρισμα μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑρμηνείας· Pete non solum linguæ donum, verum etiam interpretationis. Sic quoque Maximus spiritum exponit, quod quis Psalmorum loquatur verba, eaque canat; mentem, seu sensum, νοῦν, quod intelligentiam assecutus, in illis meditetur ac oblectetur.
anchorLine: Ψάλλει τις τῷ πνεύματι (a), ὅταν μόνον τὴν προ-
en: Theodoret rightly says: by 'spirit' he means the gift, and by 'mind' the clarity of what is said; 'spirit' he calls the gift, 'mind' the explanation of what is said. Chrysostom (hom. 35) says likewise: ask to have not only the gift of tongue but also of interpretation. Maximus likewise explains 'spirit' as a man reciting and singing the words of the Psalms, and 'mind' (nous) as the sense, by which, having grasped the meaning, he meditates and delights in them.

text: Ὁ προηγούμενος σκοπός. Voluntas scilicet Dei antecedens, τὸ προηγούμενον θέλημα, ut Damasc. loquitur post Chrys. nostrique cum illis theologi: quasi Dei a se voluntas, non nostro reatu ac causa. Opinio hæc non futuræ nuptialis copulæ Adamo non peccante, totidem pene verbis habetur in Corderiana Psalmi paraphrasi. Ἐπεὶ προηγουμένως ἦν σκοπὸς τῷ Θεῷ, μὴ διὰ γάμου γενέσθαι ἡμᾶς καὶ φθορᾶς, κ. τ. ἑ. Quandoquidem Dei primario scopus erat (destinata scilicet voluntas) ut non nuptiarum copula ac corruptione procrearemur. Sic Euseb. in Cat.: Μακάριον ἦν, τὸ μηδὲ τὴν πρώτην γυναῖκα παραβῆσαι, μηδὲ τῇ φθαρτῇ γενέσει διακονήσασθαι· μένειν δὲ ἐν παραδείσῳ θείοις ὠμοιωμένην ἀγγέλοις, κ. τ. ἑ. Beatum erat primam mulierem nec transgressam esse, nec ortui corruptibili (qui scilicet ex corruptione est ac in corruptionem ducit) ministrasse; sed ut divinis angelis facta similis maneret, etc. Nec aliter Amphil. in Symeonem et Annam, Greg. Nyss. De opificio hominis, aliisque; exque illis passim Maximus et Damasc. Nempe senserunt illi theologi, non deesse Deo alios humanæ propagationis modos, uti etiam innumeros angelorum, nulla aliorum ex aliis successione, produxit populos; eique adeo, qui jam viget, ac cum brutis animantibus nobis communis est, peccati reatu hominem addixisse. Vocem ἐκίσσησε exponit Suid. eodem ipso Maximi sensu, ex ipso hoc Psalmi loco. Nec Hebr. abhorrent יחמתני, calore concepit, catulivit. Vel quod passivum, et verbum niphal, a me calefacta est (meo scilicet conceptu). Sym. ἐκύησε, quod est in utero habere, prægnantem esse: addit Hesych. et γεννᾶν. Etiam Opp. de Venat. l. iii ἐκυήσσατο, pro peperit. Κυήσσατο τοξεύτειρα Ἀρμενίη. Unde in Cat. Hermolai Barbari Theodoretus Sym. et Aquil. tribuit, cum dolore parturiit me mater; sive peperit. Maximi hoc caput relatum inter alias Cæsarii interrogationes et respons. ejusdem Maximi nomine.
anchorLine: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ προηγούμενος σκοπὸς (b) τοῦ Θεοῦ ἦν,
en: 'The antecedent purpose': that is, God's antecedent will, as Damascene says after Chrysostom, and our theologians with them: God's will in itself, not arising from our guilt and cause. This opinion, that Adam, had he not sinned, would not have had a future marriage union, is held in almost the same words in the Cordier paraphrase of the Psalm. [Greek and its Latin version: since God's primary purpose was that we should not be born through marriage and corruption.] So Eusebius in the Catena: [it would have been blessed that the first woman not transgress nor serve a corruptible birth, but remain in paradise like the angels]. Gregory of Nyssa (On the Making of Man) and others thought likewise, and Maximus and Damascene draw from them: those theologians held that God was not without other modes of human propagation, as He produced innumerable peoples of angels with no succession of one from another, and that the mode now in force, common to us with brute animals, was assigned to man by the guilt of sin. Suidas explains the word ekissesen with the same sense of Maximus, from this very Psalm passage. The Hebrew does not shrink from 'conceived in heat, whelped'; or since the verb is passive (niphal), 'was warmed by me' (by my conception). Symmachus has ekyese, 'to have in the womb, to be pregnant'; Hesychius adds 'to beget'. Oppian too (Hunting 3) uses ekyessato for 'bore'. Hence in the Catena of Hermolaus Barbarus Theodoret attributes to Symmachus and Aquila 'with pain my mother bore me', or 'bore'. This chapter of Maximus is also included among the Interrogations and Responses of Caesarius under the same Maximus's name.

text: Παραδοθῆναι. Aliquid altius cogitavit Chrysostomus hom. 16, in illis verbis Pauli, serio excussa vi vocis ἀνάθημα et ἀνάθεμα· quæ utraque separationem sonat; altera, ob Dei reverentiam, qua sic separata quæ illi consecrata sunt, ut nemo jam contingere audeat, aut in communes usus revocare; altera, ob exsecrationem, et quod sic a Deo et Ecclesia quispiam sit abjunctus. Sic itaque Paulus, quo in Christum ardebat amore, si fieri posset, χωρισθῆναι τοῦ περὶ τὸν Χριστὸν χοροῦ, καὶ ἀλλοτριωθῆναι, οὐχὶ τῆς ἀγάπης αὐτοῦ (μὴ γένοιτο· ἐπεὶ καὶ ταῦτα δι' ἀγάπην ἐποίει)· ἀλλὰ καὶ [continues on p-0398]
anchorLine: Πυχόμην, φησὶ, παραδοθῆναι (c) ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ·
en: 'To be delivered up': Chrysostom (hom. 16) thought something deeper on Paul's words, seriously weighing the force of anathema and anathema (two spellings), each meaning separation: one through reverence for God, things so set apart as consecrated to Him that no one may touch them or call them back to common use; the other through execration, as one cut off from God and the Church. So Paul, in his love for Christ, if it could be, to be separated from the choir around Christ and estranged (not from His love, God forbid, for even this he did out of love), but also [continued on next page].

text: τῆς ἀπολαύσεως ἐκείνης καὶ τῆς δόξης, κατεδεξάμην ἄν, ὥστε μὴ τὸν δεσπότην βλασφημηθῆναι τὸν ἐμόν· Libens habuissem ab eo choro separari qui est circa Christum, fierique extraneum, non ab ejus dilectione (absit; nam et illa causa erat cur hoc faceret) sed a fruitione illa et claritate, ut Dominus meus non blasphemaretur; ex eo scilicet quod Israelitæ, electus olim populus, ad salutem per eum non adducebantur. Sic quoque Theodoret.
en: [...the Greek:] of that enjoyment and glory, I would have accepted it, so that my Lord should not be blasphemed. Latin: I would gladly have been separated from the choir around Christ and made a stranger, not from His love (God forbid; for this too was the reason he would do it) but from that enjoyment and splendour, so that my Lord should not be blasphemed; namely because the Israelites, the formerly chosen people, were not being led to salvation through Him. So also Theodoret.

text: Τὸ ἀσσάριον δεκάνουμον. Varin. Ἀσσάριον, πεντανούμιον, ἢ δεκανούμμον, prout scilicet vel pro antiquo asse sumitur, vel pro novo atque minuto. Ut enim Fr. Lucas, Fuit assarius dimidia pars assis, quem testatur percussum leg. Papiria Plinius l. xxxiii, c. 3. Lucæ interpr. pro asse integro accepit xii, 6. Οὐχὶ πέντε στρουθία ἀσσαρίων δύο πωλεῖται· cum reddit, Dipondio veneunt. Assaria ista valde minuta esse oportuit, atque ærea, quæ tot nummos, sive obolos continerent. Erant vero decem asses denarius. Corderius, apud quem exstat hic Maximi locus Matth. x, pro δεκάνουμον, δεκάλογον habet, ac decoquit; quasi sit decalogus, nummus ille, moneta, denarius quo redempti a Christo intelligimur, ex mysterio numeri denarii, ejusque nominis littera initiali. Nec unus Cord. error, quem tantisper excuset libri mendum: crassior est, qui sequitur, ἐξαγοράζεται οὖν, Veneunt igitur per nomen ejus, etc. Imo certe, venditi, per ejus nomen redimuntur. Plures de re nummaria, deque veterum nummorum, qui in Scriptura habentur, reductione ad eam monetam, qua nunc utimur. Verum hæc nobis sufficiant ad Maximi institutum.
anchorLine: Φασὶ τινὲς τὸ ἀσσάριον δεκάνουμον (d) εἶναι. Δη-
en: 'The assarion of ten coins': variant: assarion, 'of five coins', or 'of ten coins', according as it is taken for the old as or for the new, smaller one. For as Fr. Lucas says, the assarius was half of an as, attested by the Papirian law, Pliny 33.3. The Lucan translator took it for a whole as (Luke 12:6): 'Are not five sparrows sold for two assaria?' where he renders 'they are sold for a dipondius'. These assaria must have been very small and of bronze, containing so many coins or obols; ten asses made a denarius. Cordier, in whom this passage of Maximus appears (on Matt. 10), has 'decalogue' for 'ten-coin' and elaborates: as if the coin were a 'decalogue', the denarius by which we understand ourselves redeemed by Christ, from the mystery of the number ten and its initial letter. Nor is this Cordier's only error, which a misprint in his book might excuse for the moment; the following is cruder: 'is bought off, therefore', rendered 'they are sold therefore through his name'. Rather, certainly, those sold are redeemed through His name. More on the coinage and on the old coins found in Scripture, reduced to the money we now use. But let this suffice for Maximus's purpose.

text: Ὁ Θεὸς Ἀφφοῦ. Edita, ἀφφώ· unus cod. ἀπφοῦ. Procopii interpr. ampho. Hebr. אף הוא Ipse etiam; et ut Vulg. Etiam num. Syr. Ah Domine Deus domini mei Eliæ. Arab. Suscipe deprecationem meam, Domine Deus Eliæ. Theodor. et Procop. aiunt alios interpretatos, ὁ κρύφιος, Deus occultus, qui hominibus inaspectus sit et inaccessus; quod Maximus ad Eliam retulit, ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ κρυβέντος, Deus illius qui sublatus ab oculis est et jam occultus; id est, Deus Eliæ: quod ipsum voluerint Syr. et Arab. pro periphrasi nominis, ipsum proprium nomen reddentes; sitque ab אפף, quod est, circumdedit, etc., ut quæ videntur diversæ, una interpretatio, unus sensus sit.
anchorLine: τῷ Ἠλιοῦ ῥηθέν· «Ποῦ ὁ Θεὸς Ἀφφοῦ (e);»
en: 'The God of Apphou': the printed editions read aphpho; one codex has apphou. Procopius's version has 'ampho'. Hebrew: 'he also'; and as the Vulgate, 'Even now'. Syriac: 'Ah Lord, God of my lord Elijah.' Arabic: 'Receive my supplication, Lord God of Elijah.' Theodoret and Procopius say others interpreted it 'the hidden one', God hidden, inaccessible and unseen by men; Maximus referred it to Elijah: 'the God of the one who was hidden', God of him who has been taken from sight and is now hidden, that is, the God of Elijah; which the Syriac and Arabic intended as a periphrasis of the name, giving the proper name itself; and it may derive from the Hebrew root 'to surround', so that what seem different are one interpretation, one sense.

text: Κατὰ πόσους τρόπους. Non satis exsecutus Maximus, quod postulat titulus; quot modis dicta allegoria, allato duntaxat unius generis exemplo, rebus inanimatis, in quibus illud illustrius est: sed non in eis solum versatur allegoria, ut liquet ex Epist. ad Hebræos, in qua Paulus alia exponit per allegoriam; quæ scilicet Novi Testamenti fuerunt figura. Suid. Ἀλληγορία, ἡ μεταφορά· ἄλλο λέγον τὸ γράμμα, καὶ ἄλλο τὸ νόημα. Cum præter sensum quem verba ingerunt, spiritalis alius intelligitur, ipse ab Spiritu sancto præcipue intentus. Hesych. τροπολογίαν exponit τὴν ἀλληγορίαν. Ita sæpe confunduntur τὸ, ἀλληγορικῶς et τὸ τροπικῶς. quod figurate reddatur; quandoque etiam moraliter, quasi tropologia sermo moribus componendis institutus, qui τρόποι Græcis dicuntur; idcirco forsitan ἀπὸ τοῦ τρέπεσθαι, quod morum facilis sit mutatio. Sic certe Suid. Τροπολογία, ἀλλοίωσις ἑτέρου πρὸς ἕτερον κατά τι. Commutatio unius cum altero secundum aliquam rationem: καθ' ἓν τῶν ὑποκειμένων τριῶν νοημάτων, λέξεως καὶ μέλους. Malim λέξεων καὶ μελῶν, ut etiam Maximus, exemplum ponit ἐπὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων μελῶν· quod qui reddat, in nostris carminibus, velut reddit Portus, Secundum unum subjectorum trium, sententiarum, dictionis et carminis, plane ridiculus sit. Est sane tropologia, ipsaque illustrior, in membris humanis, cujus præcipue exempla exstant in Cantico canticorum: nihilque novum aut insolens, quod tria illa sic assignata sunt, in quibus versetur tropologia, conceptus, dictiones et voces humana membra; nec porro necesse fuit N. L. tanquam pro rei novitate, ascribere.
anchorLine: Κατὰ πόσους τρόπους (f) αἱ ἀλληγορίαι· καὶ τί
en: 'In how many ways': Maximus has not fully carried out what the title promises, how many ways allegory is spoken of, giving only one kind of example, from inanimate things, where it is clearest; but allegory is not confined to these, as is clear from the Epistle to the Hebrews, in which Paul explains other matters through allegory, matters which were a figure of the New Testament. Suidas: allegory is a metaphor, the letter saying one thing and the meaning another, when beyond the sense that the words convey another spiritual sense is understood, chiefly intended by the Holy Spirit. Hesychius explains tropology as allegory. So 'allegorically' and 'tropically' are often confused, which is rendered 'figuratively', and sometimes also 'morally', as if tropology were discourse set up for ordering morals (tropoi in Greek), perhaps from 'to be turned', because morals change easily. So Suidas: tropology is the alteration of one thing into another in some respect; the exchange of one with another according to some relation, by one of three underlying senses, of word and of melody. The editor would prefer 'of words and of members' (as Maximus also gives an example concerning our members); whoever should render this 'in our songs', as Portus does ('according to one of three subjects: sentences, diction and song') would be quite ridiculous. There is indeed a tropology, even a more illustrious one, in human members, whose chief examples are in the Song of Songs; nothing new or unusual that those three are so assigned in which tropology works: concepts, words and human members; nor was it necessary for 'N. L.' to ascribe it to novelty of the subject.

text: Τῷ υἱῷ τῆς μητρός. Videtur Maximus quasi sapientiæ filium dicere. Pressius Orig. fratrem. Fideles ex gentibus: filium matris, sive couterinum, qui ex circumcisione, interpretatus est: quos ipsos Judæi subvertere studeant.
anchorLine: τῆς μητρὸς (g) σκάνδαλον.
en: 'To the son of the mother': Maximus seems to say, as it were, a son of wisdom. Origen is closer: a brother. He interprets the faithful from the Gentiles as 'son of the mother' or 'of the same womb', those from the circumcision: whom the Jews themselves would strive to subvert.

text: Διὰ τῆς τῶν ἀγαθῶν. Paulo hæc humanius dicta, ac nonnullis visionibus comprobata, de illa bonorum malorumque operum comparatione, ac quasi ex lance ac trutina appensione, non sic accipienda velut aliquis gravis alicujus sceleris, ulliusve peccati, quod mortale vocant, reus, pro Dei tribunali misericordiam consequatur, pro meritorum atque virtutum majori cumulo, cum jam e vivis excesserit (aperta Dei sententia in contrarium est Ezech. xviii et xxxiii, ac fides catholica) [continues on p-0400]
anchorLine: ῥίῳ τῆς κρίσεως ἔρχονται, κἀκεῖ διὰ τῆς τῶν ἀγαθῶν (h) καὶ φαύλων πράξεων ἀντεξετάσεως οἱονεὶ πυρού-
en: 'Through the [testing] of good [and bad deeds]': these words, said by Paul in a rather human way and confirmed by some visions, about that comparison of good and bad works, as it were weighed in a balance, are not to be taken as if someone guilty of a grave crime or of some sin they call mortal obtained mercy at God's tribunal on account of a greater heap of merits and virtues when he has already departed this life (God's plain sentence is to the contrary, Ezek. 18 and 33, and the Catholic faith) [continued on next page].

text: sed solum qui minora, et quæ Dei amicitiam non penitus excludant; sive etiam qui dum adhuc vivit majorum reatum pœnitentia diluerit. Hoc etiam dicta hæc visionesque admonent, propensa bonitate indulgere, seu pœnitentiam concedere, ei cujus bona opera longe peccata excedant, etsi gravia et mortalia: sola tamen indulgentia, ac quadam velut æquitate, non ulla certa lege, ac quæ Deum ullo modo astringat. Altiora Dei judicia, ipsaque justa, cum unius peccati reum vivis sublatum æternis addicit suppliciis, tametsi vitam omnem sanctis operibus duxerat. Totam πύρωσιν, igneque probationem seu purgationem Maximus referre videtur ad judicii ἀντεξέτασιν· quæ sit ignis metaphoricus; ipse nimirum pavor, quem discussio illa de eventu suspensis ac sententia judicis ingerit; probrum etiam conscientiæ, aliaque animi propria qua animus est; ac quibus maximum animorum cruciatum esse, haud inficiandum. In Diadoci illo capite, dicuntur illi sic igne examinati, sortes sibi debitas pro ratione factorum a Deo recipere; vel scilicet ærumnam vel requiem; ærumnam æternaque supplicia, quorum malis depressa lanx fuerit; qui majora scilicet commiserint, nec pœnitentia diluerint; requiem vero, quorum bonis; qui vel minora peccaverint, vel majora pœnitendo diluerint; alicujus duntaxat pœnæ rei, quam ignis illa conflagratione in judicio Inant, et sic τῆς κολάσεως καθαίρονται, vel, supplicio liberantur; ut est apud Herod. l. v, καθαίρεσθαι πονηρῶν ἀνθρώπων. vel subintel. διά, supplicio, pœna purgantur, quod τῷ καθαρτηρίῳ mire favet, ac duos laudatos auctores, alterumque probe antiquum, habet.
note: left-margin initial words of several lines are blackened/partly illegible at the plate; transcribed as legible. The right foot column opens directly with the Greek quotation after 'l. v,'.
en: [...] but only those who committed lesser sins that do not wholly exclude God's friendship, or even one who while still alive washes away the guilt of greater sins by penance. These sayings and visions also admonish that out of propense goodness [God] may indulge or grant penance to one whose good works far exceed his sins, even grave and mortal ones: yet by indulgence alone and a kind of equity, not by any fixed law that binds God. God's higher judgments, though just, consign a man guilty of one sin, taken from the living, to eternal punishments, even if he had spent his whole life in holy works. Maximus seems to refer the whole 'fire' and the testing or purgation by fire to the examination of judgment, as a metaphorical fire: the very dread that that scrutiny, in suspense about the outcome and the judge's verdict, brings; also the disgrace of conscience and other things proper to the mind as mind; that this is the greatest torment of souls cannot be denied. In that chapter of Diadochus those so examined by fire are said to receive their due lots according to their deeds from God, either affliction or rest: affliction and eternal punishments for those whose scale is weighed down with evils, who committed greater sins without washing them away by penance; rest for those whose scale holds goods, who either sinned lightly or washed away greater sins by penance; guilty only of some penalty, which they undergo through the burning of that fire at the judgment, and so are cleansed of punishment, or freed by punishment, as in Herodotus book 5: [Greek] 'to be cleansed of wicked men'; or understand 'through': they are purged by punishment, which strongly favours the cleansing fire; and [the editor] has two cited authors, one of them truly ancient.

text: Ὑβριστικῶς. Chrysostomus ad eum Matth. locum vim maximam increpationis in illis verbis agnoscit, μετὰ τοσαύτης σφοδρότητος ἐπετίμησεν αὐτῷ· vocavitque Dominus Satanam, quod Satanæ (id est adversarii) præstaret opus, et ut ipsum ac socios ab ea serio mente deterreret: καὶ γὰρ ἐπιθυμία ἦν τοῦ ἀντικειμένου, τοῦ μὴ παθεῖν τὸν Χριστόν. Interpret. Hæc enim illius oppositi voluntas erat, ut non pateretur Christus. Cord. Cupiebat enim adversarius non pati Christum. Ego sic, Erat adversarii (Satanæ scilicet et diaboli) desiderium, ut Christus non pateretur, Τὸ μὴ παθεῖν με τῆς τοῦ διαβόλου γνώμης ἐστίν Diaboli consilium est atque animus, quod non patiar. Hoc itaque Dominus, καθικνούμενος αὐτοῦ, carpens Petrum, eumque suggillando ad officium revocans; nec video ut non sit in illis verbis aliquid ὕβρεως, vel non liceat ὑβριστικόν aliquid usurpare, tum præsertim, cum juxta subditum increpandi ac submordendi ratio est, ut saniorem illi sensum ingeras. Sic Paulus, O insensati Galatæ, etc. Galat. iii, 1. Habet Corderii Catena Μάρκου ἀσκητοῦ, nomine, eodem sensu, ac pene verbis, istud Maximi caput, etsi paulo brevius; ex quo Maximus accipere potuit ac dilatare, sicut illius capita νηπτικὰ in sua alia ducentena capita transtulit.
anchorLine: Οὐχ ὥς τινες νομίζουσι τὸν Πέτρον ἀπειλῶι Σατανᾶν ὑβριστικῶς (i) ὁ Κύριος· ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ αἱ τοῦ
en: 'Insultingly': Chrysostom recognises the greatest force of rebuke in those words of Matthew, 'with such vehemence he rebuked him'; and the Lord called him Satan because he was doing the work of Satan (the adversary), and to deter him and his companions from it earnestly: 'for it was the desire of the adversary that Christ not suffer.' The translator: 'for this was the will of that adversary, that Christ not suffer.' Cordier: 'for the adversary desired that Christ not suffer.' I read it thus: it was the wish of the adversary (Satan, the devil) that Christ not suffer; 'my not suffering is of the devil's mind' means 'it is the devil's counsel and intention that I not suffer'. So the Lord, striking at him, rebuking Peter and calling him back to duty by chiding; nor do I see that there is not something of insult in those words, or that it is not permitted to use something insulting, especially when the ground for rebuking and chiding an inferior is to instil a sounder sense in him. So Paul: 'O foolish Galatians' (Gal. 3:1). The Catena of Cordier has this chapter of Maximus under the name of Mark the Ascetic, in the same sense and almost the same words, though somewhat shorter; from it Maximus could have taken and expanded it, as he transferred that author's 'nepsis' chapters into his other collection of two hundred chapters.

anchorLine: δόξαν. Ὡς οὖν [Ἴσ. πρός] ἀντικειμένην αὐτοῦ τὴν
en: Conjecture: the siglum 'Ἴσ.' (Ἴσως, 'perhaps') marks 'πρός' as a conjectural supply (or conjectured reading) before 'ἀντικειμένην'; the editor's lettered notes on this page do not say which he prefers.

text: Τῇ ἐπιγνώσει, οὐ τῇ μεθέξει τῶν ἀγαθῶν. Hoc Maximus, damnatam Origenis et sequacium ἀποκατάστασιν, lenit, ut aliquid habere videatur sensus catholici, fiatque in specie satis Gregorii Nysseni locis, alias eo argumento perplexis ac lubricis. Haud tamen assequor, quid opus sit, longa illo sæculorum duratione, παρατάσει αἰώνιων, ad malitiæ abjiciendam memoriam, præsertim in animis. Videndus ipse Maximus ad locos Gregorii difficiles, ubi Origenianam ἀποκατάστασιν serio ex propriis elidit; præsertim ad Orat. de amore pauperum fecit Origenis assidua lectio, ut vel affinis ejus quædam expressio, ipsius aliquid furfuris nonnullis Patrum, ac in illis Nysseno, aspersisse videretur. Certe caput illud xxi de Opificio hominis, quo maxime respexisse Maximus videatur, difficillimum est; dum illo probat necessarium esse mali finem, ac qui illo moveatur, velut qui in tenebris motu feratur, necessario tandem ad bonum evasurum ac lucem; ejus exemplo qui omni terræ umbra superata, ad solis demum lucem perveniat, videaturque Maximi ipsa solutio subtilior, quam verior. Nec video posse aliter catholice exponi Nyssenum, quam ut intelligatur συνεκδοχικῶς locutus, tribuens naturæ, quod in ea clectorum sit; quibus reipsa πάλιν παράδεισος, πάλιν τὸ ξύλον ἐκεῖνο, ὃ δὴ καὶ ζωῆς ἐστι ξύλον. κ. τ. ἑ. Rursus paradisus; rursus arbor illa, quæ utique arbor est vitæ. Rursus imaginis gratia, imperiique præstantia: quod ipsum non ex vitæ præsentis usu sit, sed ἑτέρας τινὸς βασιλείας ἡ ἐλπίς, ἧς ὁ λόγος ἐν ἀπορρήτοις μένει· alterius cujusdam regni exspectatio, cujus sermo et ratio arcana manet: regni scilicet in cœlis ac spiritalis cum Christo, quæ vera nostra ἀποκατάστασις est, et in integrum restitutio.
anchorLine: Τῇ ἐπιγνώσει, οὐ τῇ μεθέξει τῶν ἀγαθῶν (j), ἀπολαβεῖν
en: 'By knowledge, not by participation in goods': Here Maximus softens the condemned apokatastasis of Origen and his followers, so that it seems to have something of Catholic sense, and it becomes, in appearance, quite like the passages of Gregory of Nyssa, otherwise perplexing and slippery on this subject. Yet I do not grasp what need there is, by that long duration of ages, 'extension of the ages', for casting away the memory of malice, especially in souls. Maximus himself must be consulted on the difficult passages of Gregory, where he seriously rejects the Origenist apokatastasis from Gregory's own words; especially in the Oration on the love of the poor, constant reading of Origen made it seem that some similar expression of his, some of his chaff, had been scattered over some Fathers, and among them Nyssa. Certainly that chapter 21 of On the Making of Man, which Maximus seems chiefly to have had in view, is most difficult, since in it he proves that an end of evil is necessary, and that one moved by it, like one carried in motion in darkness, must finally come out to the good and the light, as one who, having passed the shadow of the earth, at last arrives at the sun's light; and Maximus's own solution seems more subtle than true. Nor do I see that Nyssa can be explained in any other Catholic way than as speaking by synecdoche, attributing to nature what is in the elect; to whom in fact there is again a paradise, again that tree which is also the tree of life, etc. Again paradise; again that tree which is surely the tree of life. Again grace of the image and excellence of rule: which is not from the use of the present life but the hope of another kingdom, whose account remains among the unspeakable things: the expectation of some other kingdom whose word and reasoning remain secret: namely the kingdom in the heavens and spiritual with Christ, which is our true apokatastasis, and restoration to the whole.

text: indignantis aut spernentis, uti exposuit Basil. Gravem injuriam existimat Photius, quod quis fidelem fatuum vocet, quod hæc injuria ejus sit, qua fidelis est et Christianus, quos omnes φρονίμους decet appellari et σοφούς· prudentes et sapientes, non fatuos et stupidos. רקה, seu רקא Syriac. si quidem est κενός, quasi vacui cerebri, Hebr. haud minor injuria est, quam fatui
note: left-margin initial letters of several lines blackened at the plate; read as legible; Hebrew words transcribed as printed (small type, vowel points not resolved)
en: [...of motion] of one indignant or scornful, as Basil explained. Photius thinks it a grave insult that anyone call a faithful man a fool, because this is an insult to him as faithful and Christian, all of whom should be called prudent (phronimoi) and wise (sophoi), not fools and stupid. Raqa, or raqa in Syriac, if indeed it means 'empty', as of an empty brain; in Hebrew it is no less an insult than 'fool'.

text: Ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου. Chrysost. hom. 4 in Matth. ubi dixerat, tanquam de re nova et insolita extraque omnem exspectationem, dictum esse: Inventa est in utero habens de Spiritu sancto, μὴ περαιτέρω χώρει, μηδὲ ζήτει πλέον τι τῶν εἰρημένων. Noli ulterius procedere, neve aliud quid quæras, præter ea quæ dicta sunt. Εἰπὼν τὸν ἐργασάμενον τὸ θαῦμα, ἀπηλλάγη. Οὐδὲν γὰρ οἶδα, φησὶ, πλέον, ἀλλ' ἢ ὅτι ἐκ Πνεύματος γέγονε τὸ γεγεννημένον. Anian. Dixit quis mirabile illud effecerit, atque a cunctis pariter quæstionibus compendio liberat. Nihil enim, inquit, novi amplius, quam a sancto Spiritu factum esse, quod natum est. Auctor Imperfecti Spiritum sanctum exponit ipsum Verbum ac Filium, qui animam et corpus, templum denique (humanam scilicet naturam, quam assumpsit) condiderit. In quo tamen minime Sabellianum esse, qui Anomæus potius audiat vel Macedonianus, productis ejus Serm. in Bibl. PP. concionat. ostendi. Liquet certe totam Trinitatem Christi animam condidisse ac ejus corpus formasse, cui tandem id personæ appropries. Passim Græci de Filio τὸ ὑπεστήσατο, quod melius reddas, ibi condidit, quam illud quorumdam barbarum, suppositavit. Scite illud καταβληθῆναι, quasi de conditione ac creatione, quomodo mundi καταβολὴ Vulg. constitutio dicitur; quasi scilicet projectio ac fundatio: in qua voce Orig. sui passim erroris male præsidium quærit, quasi animi et cœlo projecti in corpora sint, non in eis recens creentur, tum cum aliquem nasci contigerit. Non satis explicat Maximus, an ipse, vel ii ex quorum sensu loquitur, existimaverint, fieri animam ex traduce, cum anima Christi, cui semen non præivit, immediate a Deo fuerit condita; et an vis seminis, ipsam animæ substantiam attingat, aut ejus solum unionem ad corpus: quod olim anceps fuit; modo non licet creationem in dubium vocare. De quo S. Thom. i, q. 90, art. 2.
anchorLine: Φασί τινες τῶν ἁγίων, ὅτι ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου (l)
note: left-margin initial letters of many lines blackened (e.g. 'Inventa', 'Matth.', 'extraque', 'Verbum', 'Sabellianum', 'Macedonianus'); read where legible; the text reads straight on from the left to the right foot column ('erroris' / 'male præsidium').
en: 'From the Holy Spirit': Chrysostom, hom. 4 on Matthew, where he had said, as of something new, unusual and beyond all expectation: 'She was found with child of the Holy Spirit': do not go further, nor seek anything beyond what has been said. Having named the one who wrought the wonder, he is done; for I know nothing more, he says, except that what was begotten came from the Spirit. Anianus: [Matthew] says who accomplished that marvel, and frees from all questions in short order. 'Nothing new, he says, beyond that what was born was made by the Holy Spirit.' The author of the Imperfect Work explains the Holy Spirit as the Word and Son himself, who built soul and body, a temple (the human nature he assumed). In which he is by no means Sabellian, but is rather to be called Anomoean or Macedonian, as shown by passages of his sermon in the Bibliotheca Patrum. It is clear that the whole Trinity created Christ's soul and formed his body, though the act is appropriated to one person. The Greeks everywhere say of the Son 'hypestesato', better rendered 'founded' than the barbarous 'suppositavit'. 'Katablethenai' is well said, as of the foundation and creation, as the 'katabole' of the world is called 'constitution' in the Vulgate; as if 'projection and foundation': in which word Origen seeks a poor defence of his error, as if souls were cast down from heaven into bodies, not created new in them when someone is born. Maximus does not explain enough whether he himself, or those from whose sense he speaks, thought the soul comes by traduction, since Christ's soul, for which no seed preceded, was created immediately by God; and whether the power of seed reaches the substance of the soul itself or only its union with the body: which was formerly doubtful; now it is not permitted to doubt creation. On this see St Thomas, Part 1, q. 90, art. 2.

text: Τῶν πρὸ τῆς ἐπιδημίας. Verius loqui Paulum de ipsis fidelibus, seu qui jam in Christum crediderant, velut apostoli, ac reliquis exemplo erant. De se enim suique similibus loquitur Paulus, Εἰς τὸ εἶναι ἡμᾶς εἰς ἔπαινον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, τοὺς προηλπικότας ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ. Ut simus in laudem ejus nos, qui ante speravimus in Christo. Ubi bene Theodoret.: Πάντες γὰρ εἰς ἡμᾶς ὁρῶντες, τοὺς εἰς τὸν Δεσπότην πεπιστευκότας, Χριστὸν ἀνυμνοῦσι, τὴν τοιούτων αἴτιον ἀγαθῶν· Omnes in nos aspicientes, qui in Dominum credidimus, Christum laudant talium bonorum auctorem. Nihil igitur ibi Paulus de sanctis veteris testam. seu ante Christum. Quod ait Maximus ἐκ μέρους; partim natura cognovisse mysterium incarnationis, seu humanæ instaurationis, φυσικῶς, affine est illi, quod ait Paulus Rom. ii, 14, de gentibus facientibus φύσει, natura seu naturaliter, opus legis; quasi scilicet ex instinctu absque legis doctrina; non tamen sine interiori afflatu, Deique per Christum gratia, quæ ipsa natura dicitur, quod Dei notitiam ejusque providentiæ solum confusam ipsique naturæ affinem tribuat: quæ ipsa ante fidem clarius revelatam, ad salutem illis proderat.
anchorLine: Πᾶς τις τῶν ἁγίων, τῶν πρὸ τῆς ἐπιδημίας (m)
en: 'Of those before the coming': Paul more truly speaks of the faithful themselves, those who had already believed in Christ, such as the apostles and others who were examples. For Paul speaks of himself and those like him: 'that we should be to the praise of his glory, who first hoped in Christ.' Theodoret says well: all, looking to us who have believed in the Master, hymn Christ as the cause of such goods. So Paul says nothing there about the saints of the Old Testament, those before Christ. What Maximus says, 'in part', that they knew the mystery of the incarnation or of human restoration partly by nature, 'naturally', is akin to what Paul says in Rom. 2:14 of Gentiles doing by nature the works of the law: as if from instinct without the teaching of the law; yet not without an inner inspiration and God's grace through Christ, which is itself called nature, because it grants only a confused knowledge of God and his providence, kin to nature itself: and this, before faith more clearly revealed, availed them for salvation.

text: Ἡρώδης δερμάτινος. Sic passim alibi Maximus. Ut autem ita pelliceus dicatur, est a voce [Hebrew word, small type, not resolved], quod est extendit; eo quod pelles sic extentæ sint. Unde Psal. Extendens cœlum sicut pellem. Georg. Pasor. opinatur a [Hebrew word, small type, not resolved], ut sit quasi dominans. Verum non sunt hæc majoris operæ. Quæstio hæc ex Regio. cod. mutila.
anchorLine: Ἡρώδης δερμάτινος (n) ἑρμηνεύεται· χρὴ οὖν τοὺς
en: 'Herod the leathern': so Maximus everywhere else. That he is so called 'leathern' comes from a word meaning 'he stretched out', because skins are so stretched; hence the Psalm: 'stretching out the heaven like a skin'. Georg. Pasor thinks it comes from another word, so as to mean 'ruling'. But these matters are of no great weight. This Question is mutilated in the Royal codex.

text: Σάρξ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπιθυμία. Sic quidem Maximus amica ubique tropologia. Alioqui plana Apostoli littera: carnem et sanguinem, naturam scilicet mortalem, quandiu mortalis est, non posse regnum cœlorum adipisci; proinde ut illo potiatur, transmutandam ad immortalitatem ac incorruptionem; quod toto illo capite contendit Paulus. Sicque bene Theodoretus.
anchorLine: Σάρξ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπιθυμία (o)· οἶμαι δὲ, ὁ θυμός.
en: 'The flesh is desire': so indeed Maximus, ever fond of tropology. Otherwise the Apostle's plain letter is: flesh and blood, that is mortal nature, while it is mortal, cannot obtain the kingdom of heaven; so that it may possess it, it must be transmuted to immortality and incorruption, which Paul argues through that whole chapter. And so Theodoret rightly.

text: Διάψαλμα. Laboraverunt in ea voce olim Orig. Hier. et alii; laborantque Hebræi in voce סלה, quam οἱ LXX sic transtulerunt: non facile novi aliquid addere. Hesych. eodem fere modo exponit ac Maximus. Διάψαλμα, μουσικοῦ μέλους ἢ ῥυθμοῦ, τροπῆς γινομένης, ἢ διανοίας καὶ δυνάμεως λόγου ἐναλλαγή· Cantus musici seu moduli, sensusve ac sermonis vis immutatio. R. Chim. elevationem vocis certo quodam modulo, Buxt. depressionem, certo itidem modulo, ac lenem quasi ac modulatam pausationem; prout quisque ab alia atque alia deducunt radice. Hieronymus ad Marcellam, magis inclinat, ut sit quasi ἐπιφώνημα et adprecatio, animique optantis expressio, uti est vox ἀμήν. quod præsertim Aquila, Hebraicarum vocum solertissimus indagator, vocem illam ubique, semper, reddiderit.
anchorLine: Τί ἐστι διάψαλμα (p);
en: 'Diapsalma': in this word Origen, Jerome and others once laboured, and the Hebrews labour over the word selah, which the Septuagint rendered thus; I cannot easily add anything new. Hesychius explains it nearly as Maximus does: 'diapsalma', a change of musical tune or rhythm, a turn occurring, or a change of thought and force of speech: the alteration of a song or measure, or of the sense and force of speech. Rabbi Kimchi takes it as a raising of the voice by a certain measure, Buxtorf as a lowering, likewise by measure, and a gentle, as it were measured, pause, according as each derives it from one root or another. Jerome (to Marcella) inclines rather to its being an epiphonema and prayer, the expression of a soul wishing, like the word 'amen'; which Aquila especially, a most skilful tracker of Hebrew words, always rendered by that word.

text: Οὗτος ὁ Λάμεχ. Sic quoque Chrys., Hom. 20 in Gen., cædes memorat. Τοὺς παρ' αὐτοῦ γενομένους φόνους ἐξαγορεῦσαι οὐ παρῃτήσατο· Cædes abs se commissas detegere ac confiteri non refugit; qua confessionis ingenuitate pœnam evasit. Eorum accepisse uxores, non meminit. Habet tamen etiam Suid. καὶ τοῦ δύο τὰς γυναῖκας εἰληφότος· νεανίσκος qui duorum accepit uxores; ipsas nimirum, quas illius uxores Scriptura memorat; videaturque ex Talmudicis acceptum. Maximus alteram sororem occisi dicit, non uxorem; næ forte quod νεανίσκος dicitur, adolescentior, quem alterum occisum existimavere, ex quibus ille accepit, ac inde non tam uxorem, quam sororem putaverunt, quas tamen per id tempus fratribus copulari nuptiali fœdere, nihil vetabat. Nihil in his certæ traditionis: sicque Theodoretus, duos a Lamecho occisos inficiatur, q. 44, sed unum eumdemque, quem Scriptura, ea repetitione, juvenem fuisse indicat, non duos esse pronuntiat: οὐ δύο, οὐδὲ τὸν Κάϊν, ὡς ἕτεροι μεμυθολογήκασιν, ἀλλ' ἕνα καὶ τοῦτον νέον. De Caino, omnium maxime olet fabulam; nec vacat temeritate, nullis prodita certioribus monumentis quasi historica fide tradere.
anchorLine: Οὗτος οὖν ὁ Λάμεχ (q) ὑπαντήσας ἀνδρὶ μετὰ τῆς γυ-
en: 'This Lamech': so also Chrysostom (Hom. 20 on Genesis) recalls the slayings: he did not decline to confess the killings he had committed; by the frankness of his confession he escaped punishment. He does not mention having taken their wives. Suidas, however, has: 'the man who took two wives', 'a young man who took the wives of two', evidently those whom Scripture mentions as his wives, and it seems drawn from the Talmudists. Maximus says the other was the sister of the slain man, not a wife; perhaps because 'neaniskos' means the younger, whom they supposed the second one slain, from whom he took, and so they thought her less a wife than a sister, though at that time nothing forbade siblings from being joined in marriage. There is nothing of certain tradition in these things: so Theodoret denies that two were killed by Lamech (q. 44), but pronounces one and the same, whom Scripture by that repetition indicates to have been a youth, not two: 'not two, nor Cain, as others have fabled, but one, and he young'. About Cain it smells most of all of fable; nor is it free of rashness to hand it down as historical when no surer records have transmitted it.
